entries.sourceText: - **1. Monty Hall** \[Predict\]: pick a door, the host opens a goat, stay or switch? Auto-play 1,000 rounds; switching wins about 2/3.
entries.title: A host who knows the prize
entries.lens: the knowledgeable host protocol

entries.sourceText: - **2. Monty Hall, 100 doors** \[Gotcha\]: the host opens 98 goat doors. Suddenly switching feels obvious, and the 3-door case clicks.
entries.title: Ninety-eight goat doors
entries.lens: the unchosen probability mass

entries.sourceText: - **3. Monty Fall** \[Gotcha\]: the host trips and opens a random door that happens to show a goat. Now it really is 50/50, because the host's knowledge was doing the work.
entries.title: The host opened a goat by accident
entries.lens: the random-host likelihood

entries.sourceText: - **4. Birthday paradox** \[Predict\]: guess how many people give a 50% chance of a shared birthday. Answer: 23. Slide to 70 for 99.9%.
entries.title: Any pair shares a birthday
entries.lens: the event of any matching pair

entries.sourceText: - **5. Your birthday** \[Split\]: half are asked about any shared birthday, half about someone sharing *theirs*. The second needs 253 people for 50%.
entries.title: Someone shares your birthday
entries.lens: a specified birthday rather than any pair

entries.sourceText: - **6. Boy or girl** \[Gotcha\]: a family has two kids, at least one a boy. Chance both are boys? 1/3, not 1/2.
entries.title: Condition on at least one boy
entries.lens: the family-level conditioning event

entries.sourceText: - **7. The Tuesday boy** \[Gotcha\]: at least one is a boy born on Tuesday. The answer jumps to 13/27, and the grid of 196 cases shows why.
entries.title: A boy in a named day category
entries.lens: the specified reporting category

entries.sourceText: - **8. Bertrand's box** \[Gotcha\]: three boxes (gold-gold, silver-silver, gold-silver). You draw gold; the other coin is gold with probability 2/3.
entries.title: Gold from a mixed box
entries.lens: the box-selection prior and gold likelihood

entries.sourceText: - **9. Three prisoners** \[Gotcha\]: a guard names one prisoner who will die. Your survival odds don't change, but the other prisoner's double.
entries.title: What the guard could have said
entries.lens: the guard's announcement protocol

entries.sourceText: - **10. Two envelopes** \[Gotcha\]: switching always seems to gain 25% in expectation. Swipe to find the broken step.
entries.title: Assign the envelopes first
entries.lens: the assignment probability before observing money

entries.sourceText: - **11. Sleeping Beauty** \[Split\]: poll viewers as "halfers" or "thirders", then show each side's best argument.
entries.title: Sample experiments or visits?
entries.lens: the unit being sampled in repeated experiments

entries.sourceText: - **12. Bertrand's chord** \[Slider\]: three ways to draw a "random" chord give answers of 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4. "Random" needs a definition.
entries.title: Two ways to randomize a chord
entries.lens: the midpoint sampling measure

entries.sourceText: - **13. Penney's game** \[Predict\]: pick a 3-flip pattern; the app always picks one that beats it, up to 7:1.
entries.title: A race between overlapping patterns
entries.lens: the suffix state in first-pattern arrival

entries.sourceText: - **14. HH vs HT** \[Predict\]: which takes more flips on average to appear? HH takes 6, HT takes 4.
entries.title: HH and HT take different times
entries.lens: prefix overlap in waiting times

entries.sourceText: - **15. Nontransitive dice** \[Predict\]: pick any of Efron's dice; the app picks one that beats yours 2/3 of the time.
entries.title: Dice can beat each other in a cycle
entries.lens: the ordered face-pair comparison

entries.sourceText: - **16. Parrondo's paradox** \[Slider\]: two games that each lose money win when alternated.
entries.title: Mixing changes the capital states
entries.lens: the stationary capital-residue distribution

entries.sourceText: - **17. The secretary problem** \[Measure\]: swipe through 100 candidates and stop on the best. Skipping the first 37% maximizes your odds.
entries.title: When to start accepting records
entries.lens: the skip threshold under random ordering

entries.sourceText: - **18. Friendship paradox** \[Gotcha\]: on average, your friends have more friends than you do. Popular people are overcounted.
entries.title: Popular friends get sampled more
entries.lens: size-weighted degree sampling

entries.sourceText: - **19. Inspection paradox** \[Gotcha\]: buses come every 10 minutes on average, yet your typical wait is longer than 5. Long gaps catch more arrivals.
entries.title: Long bus gaps catch more arrivals
entries.lens: gap-length weighting rather than uniform gaps

entries.sourceText: - **20. Coupon collector** \[Predict\]: how many packs to complete a 50-sticker album? About 225.
entries.title: The last missing sticker
entries.lens: the sum of successive collection waits

entries.sourceText: - **21. Fake the coin** \[Measure\]: type 100 "random" H/T; the app spots you're human because you avoided long runs.
entries.title: How many runs should a coin make?
entries.lens: transitions in an independent sequence

entries.sourceText: - **22. Longest streak** \[Predict\]: guess the longest run in 100 real flips. It's usually 6 or 7.
entries.title: A bound on long heads windows
entries.lens: overlap in a longest-run upper bound

entries.sourceText: - **23. Gambler's fallacy** \[Measure\]: after 5 heads, call the next flip. Your hit rate stays stubbornly at 50%.
entries.title: The coin does not owe you tails
entries.lens: independence after a specified streak

entries.sourceText: - **24. Hot hand bias** \[Gotcha\]: in 4-flip sequences, the average share of heads after heads is about 40%, not 50%.
entries.title: Average the selected short sequences
entries.lens: sequence-level averaging after heads

entries.sourceText: - **25. Shuffle feels rigged** \[Gotcha\]: truly random playlists repeat artists, which is why music apps make shuffle *less* random.
entries.title: Uniform shuffles allow repeats
entries.lens: adjacent artist repeats under uniform shuffling

entries.sourceText: - **26. Spot the random dots** \[Split\]: which pattern is random? Most pick the evenly spaced one; the clumpy one is random.
entries.title: Random points leave empty cells
entries.lens: gaps under independent uniform placement

entries.sourceText: - **27. Two-dice sums** \[Predict\]: build the histogram roll by roll; 7 wins because it has the most combinations.
entries.title: Why seven has more pairs
entries.lens: ordered pairs behind a sum

entries.sourceText: - **28. De Méré's bet** \[Predict\]: one six in 4 rolls (51.8%) vs double six in 24 rolls of two dice (49.1%).
entries.title: One six or one double six?
entries.lens: the complement over independent attempts

entries.sourceText: - **29. Waiting for a six** \[Predict\]: it takes 6 rolls on average, yet only 66.5% of the time do you get one within 6.
entries.title: A six within six rolls
entries.lens: finite-horizon success versus mean waiting time

entries.sourceText: - **30. Catch the loaded die** \[Slider\]: set the bias, roll until you're sure. Small biases need hundreds of rolls.
entries.title: A biased die produces a count
entries.lens: the likelihood of one specified count

entries.sourceText: - **31. Benford's law** \[Predict\]: guess how often real-world numbers start with 1. About 30%.
entries.title: The first digit is not uniform
entries.lens: a logarithmic leading-digit model

entries.sourceText: - **32. Pick a number 1–10** \[Split\]: see the crowd's distribution; 7 dominates and 1 and 10 are rare.
entries.title: A toy crowd favors seven
entries.lens: the group mixture behind an observed choice share

entries.sourceText: - **33. Rock-paper-scissors bot** \[Measure\]: a simple pattern-learner beats most people over 50 rounds.
entries.title: Exploit a predictable opponent
entries.lens: the payoff from an assumed response probability

entries.sourceText: - **34. Seven shuffles** \[Slider\]: it takes about 7 riffle shuffles to mix a deck well (Bayer & Diaconis, 1992).
entries.title: An ideal ten-card riffle model
entries.lens: one permutation's deviation from uniformity

entries.sourceText: - **35. 52 factorial** \[Gotcha\]: a well-shuffled deck is almost certainly in an order never seen before in history.
entries.title: Count orders on a logarithmic scale
entries.lens: the factorial number of distinct permutations

entries.sourceText: - **36. Stock or coin?** \[Split\]: guess which chart is a real stock and which is a coin-flip random walk.
entries.title: A coin walk can look like a trend
entries.lens: diffusive displacement rather than a market forecast

entries.sourceText: - **37. Lottery 1-2-3-4-5-6** \[Gotcha\]: the same odds as any combination, but thousands play it, so a win pays less.
entries.title: Share the winning lottery pot
entries.lens: the number of co-winners sharing a fixed prize

entries.sourceText: - **38. Seeds** \[Slider\]: set a pseudo-random seed and the "random" sequence repeats exactly.
entries.title: A seed reproduces the next state
entries.lens: a deterministic generator recurrence

entries.sourceText: - **39. Coins have memory of their start** \[Story\]: in about 350,000 flips, coins landed on their starting side about 50.8% of the time (Bartoš et al., 2023).
entries.title: A tiny excess over half
entries.lens: the observed share versus the proposed coin model

entries.sourceText: - **40. Monopoly heatmap** \[Predict\]: guess the most-landed square. Jail, thanks to the dice-and-card mechanics.
entries.title: A toy jail-detour chain
entries.lens: the visit rate in a stated two-state board model

entries.sourceText: - **41. Positive mammogram** \[Predict\]: 1% prevalence, 90% sensitivity, 9% false positives. Chance of cancer after a positive? About 9%.
entries.title: A positive result needs a base rate
entries.lens: true and false positives in one population

entries.sourceText: - **42. Same problem, as people** \[Split\]: half see percentages, half see "10 of 1,000 women...". The frequency half does far better.
entries.title: The same cases as proportions
entries.lens: the common-population denominator

entries.sourceText: - **43. The cab problem** \[Gotcha\]: an 80%-reliable witness says the cab was blue, but only 15% of cabs are. Real chance: about 41%.
entries.title: A witness names the rare cab
entries.lens: the cab prevalence before the witness report

entries.sourceText: - **44. Prosecutor's fallacy** \[Gotcha\]: "1 in a million chance of a match if innocent" is not "1 in a million chance of being innocent".
entries.title: A rare match is not a posterior
entries.lens: the prior odds behind a match likelihood

entries.sourceText: - **45. Defense attorney's fallacy** \[Gotcha\]: few abusers become murderers, but among murdered women with abusive partners, the partner is the likely culprit.
entries.title: Reverse the conditional carefully
entries.lens: the specified population and reverse conditional

entries.sourceText: - **46. Build a spam filter** \[Slider\]: toggle words like "free" and "invoice" and watch the spam probability update.
entries.title: A word changes spam odds
entries.lens: the likelihood ratio of a specified word

entries.sourceText: - **47. Base-rate slider** \[Slider\]: keep the test fixed, slide prevalence from 0.1% to 50%, and watch a positive result's meaning flip.
entries.title: Slide the base rate, keep the test
entries.lens: the base rate with unchanged test characteristics

entries.sourceText: - **48. Test twice** \[Predict\]: a second independent positive takes the posterior from 9% to about 50%.
entries.title: Two conditionally independent positives
entries.lens: conditional independence across repeated tests

entries.sourceText: - **49. The 99.9% terrorist detector** \[Slider\]: screen a million travelers and nearly every alarm is an innocent person.
entries.title: A rare target in a large crowd
entries.lens: the prevalence behind a highly accurate alarm

entries.sourceText: - **50. Face recognition in a stadium** \[Slider\]: even accurate matching floods police with false matches in big crowds.
entries.title: Stadium matching and false alarms
entries.lens: the target fraction in the screened crowd

entries.sourceText: - **51. Librarian or farmer?** \[Gotcha\]: a shy, tidy man is still more likely a farmer, since farmers vastly outnumber librarians.
entries.title: A description versus prior odds
entries.lens: the occupational base rate before a description

entries.sourceText: - **52. Draw the tree** \[Slider\]: drag branch widths in a probability tree and watch the posterior box resize.
entries.title: Weight the two branches of the tree
entries.lens: the prior branch widths in Bayes' rule

entries.sourceText: - **53. What a negative test means** \[Slider\]: a negative rapid test reassures less when symptoms or local prevalence are high.
entries.title: A negative test with a high prior
entries.lens: the probability left after a negative result

entries.sourceText: - **54. Three friends in Seattle** \[Predict\]: each lies 1/3 of the time; all say it's raining. With a 25% prior, the chance it's raining is about 73%.
entries.title: Three independent reports of rain
entries.lens: the conditional independence of witness reports

entries.sourceText: - **55. Lie detector** \[Slider\]: set accuracy and the share of liars; most "liars" flagged among honest crowds are false alarms.
entries.title: A lie detector in an honest crowd
entries.lens: the share of liars before a detector alarm

entries.sourceText: - **56. "70% chance of rain"** \[Gotcha\]: it means it rains on about 70% of days with that forecast, and that calibration can be checked.
entries.title: Seventy percent over repeated days
entries.lens: forecast calibration over repeated outcomes

entries.sourceText: - **57. Which urn?** \[Predict\]: draw balls one by one and watch the posterior bar between two urns shift.
entries.title: Which urn supplied the ball?
entries.lens: the likelihood ratio of a specified draw

entries.sourceText: - **58. Doping tests** \[Slider\]: with few cheaters, even a good test catches many clean athletes.
entries.title: A doping alarm in a rare class
entries.lens: the base rate among tested athletes

entries.sourceText: - **59. Early pregnancy test** \[Slider\]: the meaning of a faint positive changes with how many days late you are.
entries.title: An early test changes sensitivity
entries.lens: the sensitivity at a stated testing time

entries.sourceText: - **60. "Most crashes happen near home"** \[Gotcha\]: because most driving happens near home, not because home roads are dangerous.
entries.title: Crashes need exposure denominators
entries.lens: driving exposure rather than crash counts alone

entries.sourceText: - **61. Galton board** \[Predict\]: drop 1,000 balls through pegs and a bell curve builds itself.
entries.title: The peg board counts right turns
entries.lens: binomial paths through independent pegs

entries.sourceText: - **62. Central limit theorem** \[Slider\]: average N rolls of a weird die; as N grows, any shape turns into a bell.
entries.title: Averages shrink their sampling spread
entries.lens: the finite-variance averaging scale

entries.sourceText: - **63. Height vs wealth** \[Split\]: the tallest person is under 1.5× average height; the richest is millions of times average wealth.
entries.title: A typical value versus an extreme
entries.lens: the effect of an extreme observation on the mean

entries.sourceText: - **64. Goals per match** \[Predict\]: guess the share of 0–0 football games, then see the Poisson curve fit.
entries.title: A zero-goal toy count
entries.lens: the event-count rate in a Poisson model

entries.sourceText: - **65. Horse kicks** \[Story\]: Prussian cavalry deaths by horse kick fit a Poisson distribution almost perfectly (Bortkiewicz, 1898).
entries.title: Rare incidents per unit of exposure
entries.lens: the stated Poisson rate per exposure unit

entries.sourceText: - **66. Waiting times** \[Slider\]: set an arrival rate and watch exponential gaps: lots of short waits, a few very long.
entries.title: Short waits and a long tail
entries.lens: a constant-rate waiting-time model

entries.sourceText: - **67. The memoryless bulb** \[Gotcha\]: for a bulb with exponential lifetime, having lasted 1,000 hours doesn't shorten its remaining life.
entries.title: The age of a memoryless bulb
entries.lens: elapsed age in exponential conditional survival

entries.sourceText: - **68. Free throws** \[Slider\]: a 70% shooter takes 10 shots; see how often they hit 5 or fewer.
entries.title: Ten shots from a seventy-percent shooter
entries.lens: the complement of five-or-fewer successes

entries.sourceText: - **69. Tries until success** \[Predict\]: with a 1-in-20 chance per try, how many tries is typical? Many need far more than 20.
entries.title: Twenty tries is not a guarantee
entries.lens: finite attempts for a geometric waiting process

entries.sourceText: - **70. Zipf's law** \[Predict\]: guess the share of English text that is "the". Around 5–7%, with each next word roughly half as common.
entries.title: Normalize a finite Zipf vocabulary
entries.lens: the normalization of ranked frequency weights

entries.sourceText: - **71. 80/20** \[Slider\]: tune a Pareto distribution and see what share of the top 20% owns.
entries.title: How much does the top fifth hold?
entries.lens: the Pareto shape behind concentration

entries.sourceText: - **72. Fat tails** \[Gotcha\]: under a normal model, the 1987 one-day 20% crash was a 20-plus-sigma event that "should" never happen.
entries.title: A tail observation changes the mean
entries.lens: tail sensitivity rather than proof of a normal law

entries.sourceText: - **73. Hidden e** \[Predict\]: add random numbers between 0 and 1 until the sum passes 1. The average count is e ≈ 2.718.
entries.title: Uniform draws until the sum passes one
entries.lens: the capped waiting-time survival sum

entries.sourceText: - **74. Beta as belief** \[Slider\]: add wins and losses and watch a beta curve sharpen around a success rate.
entries.title: Wins sharpen an explicit prior
entries.lens: prior counts and observed coin data

entries.sourceText: - **75. Birthday calendar** \[Story\]: real birthdays aren't uniform; US births dip on holidays and peak in September.
entries.title: A toy calendar with fewer dates
entries.lens: the support size of a simplified birthday model

entries.sourceText: - **76. Mixed heights** \[Gotcha\]: men and women differ in average height, yet the combined distribution barely shows two humps.
entries.title: Two height groups in one mean
entries.lens: group weights without inferring histogram modality

entries.sourceText: - **77. The Cauchy average** \[Predict\]: average more and more samples and it never settles down.
entries.title: A Cauchy average keeps its scale
entries.lens: the failure of finite-variance averaging assumptions

entries.sourceText: - **78. 68–95–99.7** \[Slider\]: drag a band of ±1, 2, 3 standard deviations and watch the coverage.
entries.title: A stated normal-coverage approximation
entries.lens: the coverage as a band widens

entries.sourceText: - **79. 100-year flood** \[Gotcha\]: it has about a 26% chance of hitting during a 30-year mortgage.
entries.title: A one-percent annual flood risk
entries.lens: independent annual risk over a mortgage horizon

entries.sourceText: - **80. Name that distribution** \[Predict\]: see a histogram, guess which process made it: dice, waiting times, counts or wealth.
entries.title: A process gives the count shape
entries.lens: the mean of a specified count-generating process

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **81. Small schools** \[Gotcha\]: the smallest schools dominate both the best and the worst score lists, simply from noise.
entries.title: Small schools have noisy proportions
entries.lens: sample size behind extreme observed school rates

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **82. Kidney cancer map** \[Gotcha\]: rural counties have both the highest and lowest rates, because small populations swing wildly (Wainer, 2007).
entries.title: Small counties have variable rates
entries.lens: population exposure behind a noisy proportion

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **83. Cover jinx** \[Gotcha\]: athletes slump after magazine covers because they were featured at a lucky peak.
entries.title: A cover follows a lucky peak
entries.lens: selection on an extreme noisy score

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **84. Sophomore slump** \[Predict\]: simulate skill plus luck; the top rookies of year one mostly do worse in year two.
entries.title: The next season after a rookie peak
entries.lens: reliability in a repeat-performance model

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **85. Praise vs punishment** \[Gotcha\]: pilots improved after being yelled at for bad landings, but would have anyway.
entries.title: Improvement after a bad landing
entries.lens: regression without assigning a punishment effect

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **86. Galton's heights** \[Slider\]: very tall parents have tall kids, but less extreme ones.
entries.title: An extreme parent-height score
entries.lens: the regression coefficient in a stated height model

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **87. Margin of error** \[Slider\]: poll 100, 1,000, 10,000 people; the ±3% at 1,000 appears on its own.
entries.title: The poll margin has a square root
entries.lens: the standard error before applying an interval multiplier

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **88. City vs country** \[Gotcha\]: a poll of 1,000 is about as precise for a city of a million as for a country of 300 million.
entries.title: A city poll versus a country poll
entries.lens: the finite-population sampling fraction

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **89. Online poll** \[Split\]: show a self-selected poll beside a random sample of the same question.
entries.title: Self-selection changes the poll mix
entries.lens: selection weights rather than random-sampling precision

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **90. The square-root law** \[Slider\]: to halve the error, you need four times the sample.
entries.title: Four times the sample, half the spread
entries.lens: the square-root precision law

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **91. Lead that grows** \[Predict\]: the share of heads converges to 50%, but the gap between heads and tails count keeps growing.
entries.title: A fraction settles while counts wander
entries.lens: absolute random-walk displacement

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **92. 5.0 vs 4.8 stars** \[Split\]: 3 reviews at 5.0 or 2,000 at 4.8? Shrink each toward the average to see which is better.
entries.title: Three perfect reviews or many good ones
entries.lens: review counts in a stated shrinkage rule

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **93. Last year's best fund** \[Gotcha\]: top-performing funds mostly fall back toward average the next year.
entries.title: Last year's top fund regresses
entries.lens: an assumed repeat-return reliability

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **94. Treated when worst** \[Gotcha\]: patients enroll when symptoms peak, so they improve even with a useless treatment.
entries.title: Treatment starts at a symptom peak
entries.lens: regression before claiming treatment causation

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **95. Speed cameras** \[Gotcha\]: cameras go up after a run of crashes, so crashes fall partly by regression alone.
entries.title: A camera follows a crash spike
entries.lens: selection of sites after unusually high counts

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **96. Retake the test** \[Predict\]: bottom scorers improve and top scorers slip on a retake, with no teaching.
entries.title: A retake without new teaching
entries.lens: opposite deviations under the same repeat-score rule

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **97. Salesperson of the quarter** \[Predict\]: simulate a team of equally skilled sellers and watch "stars" rotate.
entries.title: The sales star and next quarter
entries.lens: the noise share behind selected top performers

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **98. How many to survey?** \[Slider\]: set the precision you want and get the sample size.
entries.title: Choose a desired poll half-width
entries.lens: the sample cost of tighter precision

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **99. Stratified sampling** \[Slider\]: compare random vs stratified samples of a lumpy population; stratified wobbles less.
entries.title: Strata have explicit population weights
entries.lens: the strata weights needed for an aggregate estimate

entries.sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
entries.sourceText: - **100. The Xbox poll** \[Story\]: a heavily skewed 2012 poll of Xbox users, reweighted by demographics, forecast the US election well (Wang, Rothschild, Goel & Gelman, 2015).
entries.title: Reweight the Xbox-like sample
entries.lens: the target-population mixture rather than sample composition

entries.sourceText: - **101. Is the coin fair?** \[Slider\]: flip and watch the posterior over the coin's bias narrow with each toss.
entries.title: Learn the coin's next-head probability
entries.lens: the Beta-Bernoulli predictive mean

entries.sourceText: - **102. Stubborn vs open mind** \[Slider\]: set prior strength and see how much data it takes to move each belief.
entries.title: A strong prior takes more data
entries.lens: prior strength under identical observations

entries.sourceText: - **103. Two skeptics converge** \[Predict\]: two people with opposite priors see the same data and end up agreeing.
entries.title: Opposite priors see the same evidence
entries.lens: the influence of fixed prior counts as data accumulate

entries.sourceText: - **104. Will the sun rise?** \[Gotcha\]: Laplace's rule of succession gives (n+1)/(n+2) after n sunrises, never quite 1.
entries.title: A success streak is not probability one
entries.lens: Laplace smoothing of repeated successes

entries.sourceText: - **105. German tank problem** \[Predict\]: see a few captured serial numbers and estimate how many tanks exist.
entries.title: The largest serial is not the total
entries.lens: the expected unseen gap beyond a sampled maximum

entries.sourceText: - **106. Credible vs confidence** \[Split\]: the same data, two intervals, two very different meanings.
entries.title: A posterior band uses an explicit prior
entries.lens: posterior conditioning rather than repeated-sampling coverage

entries.sourceText: - **107. Bayes factor** \[Slider\]: how many heads in a row before "trick coin" beats "fair coin"?
entries.title: Heads favor a specified trick coin
entries.lens: the likelihood ratio against a stated alternative

entries.sourceText: - **108. Automatic Occam's razor** \[Gotcha\]: a flexible model spreads its bets, so a simple model that fits wins the evidence.
entries.title: Evidence rewards concentrated prediction
entries.lens: the marginal likelihood ratio of two stated models

entries.sourceText: - **109. Bayesian average ratings** \[Slider\]: blend each product's stars with the site average, weighted by review count.
entries.title: Blend ratings with a prior mean
entries.lens: the relative weight of reviews and a prior pseudoreview

entries.sourceText: - **110. "Chance B beats A"** \[Slider\]: feed in A/B conversions and watch the posterior probability that B is better.
entries.title: B versus a uniform uncertain A
entries.lens: the special case of a uniform comparator posterior

entries.sourceText: - **111. Flat isn't neutral** \[Gotcha\]: a flat prior on a probability is not flat on its odds or log-odds.
entries.title: Uniform probability is not uniform odds
entries.lens: the nonlinear mapping from log-odds to probability

entries.sourceText: - **112. Finding a lost plane** \[Story\]: Bayesian search theory helped locate the USS Scorpion (1968) and Air France 447's wreck (2011).
entries.title: A search clue changes regional odds
entries.lens: the regional prior and clue likelihood ratio

entries.sourceText: - **113. Normal meets normal** \[Slider\]: blend a prior mean with noisy measurements and watch the posterior shift and tighten.
entries.title: Combine normal prior and measurement
entries.lens: the relative precisions in a normal update

entries.sourceText: - **114. Cromwell's rule** \[Gotcha\]: give anything a prior of exactly 0 and no evidence can ever revive it.
entries.title: A zero prior stays zero
entries.lens: the difference between impossible and merely unlikely

entries.sourceText: - **115. Doomsday argument** \[Split\]: poll whether it's convincing, then show the strongest objections.
entries.title: A stated rank-sampling assumption
entries.lens: the sampling assumption rather than a doomsday conclusion

entries.sourceText: - **116. Next free throw** \[Predict\]: predict the next shot from the full posterior, not just the best guess.
entries.title: Predict the next free throw
entries.lens: posterior prediction rather than a maximum-likelihood point

entries.sourceText: - **117. Strength of evidence** \[Slider\]: drag a likelihood ratio and see how it multiplies your prior odds.
entries.title: Multiply odds, then convert back
entries.lens: likelihood ratios on the odds scale

entries.sourceText: - **118. Three heads in a row** \[Split\]: maximum likelihood says the coin always lands heads; a Bayesian disagrees.
entries.title: Three heads with a finite prior
entries.lens: the prior behind a prediction after a short streak

entries.sourceText: - **119. Lindley's paradox** \[Gotcha\]: a result can be "significant" while the Bayesian evidence favors no effect.
entries.title: A p-value alone is not a Bayes factor
entries.lens: the prior odds in a stated Bayesian comparison

entries.sourceText: - **120. Your hidden rating** \[Predict\]: play matches and watch an Elo or TrueSkill estimate of your skill update.
entries.title: A toy hidden skill update
entries.lens: the update weight after new skill evidence

entries.sourceText: - **121. St. Petersburg game** \[Measure\]: name your price to play a game with infinite expected value. Most say under $20.
entries.title: Cap the doubling-payoff game
entries.lens: the distinction between capped expectation and typical payout

entries.sourceText: - **122. Kelly betting** \[Slider\]: choose a bet fraction on a favorable coin; too high and you go broke despite your edge.
entries.title: Bet sizing under known odds
entries.lens: the log-growth optimum under specified odds

entries.sourceText: - **123. The ergodicity coin** \[Predict\]: +50% on heads, −40% on tails. The average grows, yet almost every player ends near zero.
entries.title: Positive mean, negative compound growth
entries.lens: arithmetic versus compound return

entries.sourceText: - **124. Why insure?** \[Slider\]: a negative-expected-value policy makes sense once the utility curve bends.
entries.title: Insurance and curved utility
entries.lens: wealth-relative utility curvature in a stated model

entries.sourceText: - **125. Lottery rollover** \[Slider\]: grow the jackpot until the ticket's expected value turns positive, then add shared winners.
entries.title: Share the rollover prize
entries.lens: the split jackpot conditional on a shared win

entries.sourceText: - **126. Be the banker** \[Measure\]: play a *Deal or No Deal*-style game and see your implied risk attitude.
entries.title: An offer versus a specified gamble
entries.lens: the probability behind the cash expectation

entries.sourceText: - **127. Newcomb's problem** \[Split\]: one box or two? Show the poll, then both camps' arguments.
entries.title: A predictor's observed track record
entries.lens: the stated evidence about a predictor without resolving a decision theory

entries.sourceText: - **128. Pascal's mugging** \[Split\]: a tiny chance of an enormous payoff; poll whether to pay, then discuss.
entries.title: An enormous payoff times tiny odds
entries.lens: the explicitly assumed probability-payoff product

entries.sourceText: - **129. Mean vs median startup** \[Gotcha\]: the average outcome is great, while the typical founder gets nothing.
entries.title: A startup mean exceeds the typical case
entries.lens: an extreme success in a toy payoff distribution

entries.sourceText: - **130. Gambler's ruin** \[Slider\]: set bankrolls and edge; even a fair game ruins the poorer player most of the time.
entries.title: A small bankroll can hit zero first
entries.lens: absorbing boundaries in a fair game

entries.sourceText: - **131. Martingale roulette** \[Predict\]: double after every loss; simulate until the table limit or bankroll ends it.
entries.title: The bankroll needed after losses
entries.lens: the geometric cost of a doubling strategy

entries.sourceText: - **132. Value of information** \[Slider\]: how much should you pay for a forecast before planning a picnic?
entries.title: The upper value of a perfect forecast
entries.lens: state-contingent choices under perfect information

entries.sourceText: - **133. Selling a house** \[Slider\]: offers arrive one by one; set your threshold and see the expected price.
entries.title: A higher threshold means more waiting
entries.lens: the accepted-offer mean and waiting tradeoff

entries.sourceText: - **134. Diversification** \[Slider\]: add assets and dial their correlation; risk falls only when they don't move together.
entries.title: Correlations limit diversification
entries.lens: covariance between asset returns

entries.sourceText: - **135. Volatility drag** \[Gotcha\]: +50% then −50% leaves you with 75%.
entries.title: Up fifty, down fifty
entries.lens: multiplicative return arithmetic

entries.sourceText: - **136. Extended warranty** \[Slider\]: plug in failure rate and repair cost to see the expected loss on the warranty.
entries.title: Expected warranty saving minus price
entries.lens: the failure probability behind a warranty comparison

entries.sourceText: - **137. Bookmaker odds** \[Gotcha\]: convert odds to implied probabilities and they sum past 100%; that gap is the house edge.
entries.title: Reciprocal odds exceed one
entries.lens: the overround in an exhaustive two-outcome book

entries.sourceText: - **138. Poker bankroll** \[Slider\]: set win rate and variance; see the chance of going broke before the edge pays off.
entries.title: An edge still faces bankroll risk
entries.lens: a favorable step probability with finite bankroll

entries.sourceText: - **139. Treatment decision tree** \[Slider\]: drag probabilities and outcomes in a medical decision tree until the best option flips.
entries.title: Compare explicit expected harms
entries.lens: the stipulated risks in a decision tree

entries.sourceText: - **140. Log utility** \[Slider\]: compare linear and log utility for the same gamble and watch the preferred choice change.
entries.title: One gamble, different initial wealth
entries.lens: initial wealth in a log-utility comparison

entries.sourceText: - **141. Drunkard's walk** \[Predict\]: after n random steps, distance from start grows like √n, not n.
entries.title: Root-mean-square distance after steps
entries.lens: the square-root displacement scale

entries.sourceText: - **142. Drunk man vs drunk bird** \[Gotcha\]: a random walker in 1D or 2D always returns home; in 3D, only about 34% do (Pólya).
entries.title: Return at a finite time
entries.lens: finite endpoint return versus ever returning

entries.sourceText: - **143. Hitting the wall** \[Slider\]: move the wall closer or farther and see how long a random walk takes to reach it.
entries.title: A fair walk between two walls
entries.lens: the boundary distances in an absorption time

entries.sourceText: - **144. Snakes and ladders** \[Predict\]: guess the average game length, then solve it exactly as a Markov chain.
entries.title: One ladder, one waiting-time question
entries.lens: the chance of reaching a required die face within a horizon

entries.sourceText: - **145. Weather chain** \[Slider\]: set sunny-to-rainy odds and watch the long-run share of rainy days settle.
entries.title: A weather chain forgets its start
entries.lens: transition rates and a finite-time weather distribution

entries.sourceText: - **146. Markov text** \[Slider\]: generate text from word-pair statistics; raise the order and it starts to sound real.
entries.title: A toy word-pair model comparison
entries.lens: the likelihood ratio assigned to a specified text feature

entries.sourceText: - **147. The other line is faster** \[Gotcha\]: with three checkout lines, another one beats yours two times out of three.
entries.title: Another checkout line wins the race
entries.lens: exchangeable lines without ties

entries.sourceText: - **148. One line or many?** \[Split\]: a single shared queue cuts the worst waits compared with separate lines.
entries.title: Delay grows near service capacity
entries.lens: the load of a stated single-server queue

entries.sourceText: - **149. Phantom traffic jam** \[Slider\]: add random braking to a ring road and jams appear from nothing.
entries.title: Random service delay near saturation
entries.lens: the queueing analogy under explicit arrival and service assumptions

entries.sourceText: - **150. Brownian motion** \[Slider\]: shake a pollen grain with invisible molecules and watch it jitter.
entries.title: A diffusive toy particle
entries.lens: the variance scale of independent microscopic kicks

entries.sourceText: - **151. Arcsine law** \[Gotcha\]: in a fair coin game, one player usually leads for most of the time.
entries.title: Time ahead need not be evenly split
entries.lens: the limiting occupation-time distribution

entries.sourceText: - **152. The ballot problem** \[Predict\]: if A gets 60% of votes, what's the chance A leads throughout the count? 20%.
entries.title: Win the election and lead throughout
entries.lens: the strict lead event under random vote ordering

entries.sourceText: - **153. Ehrenfest urn** \[Slider\]: particles hop between two rooms and settle near 50/50 with fluctuations.
entries.title: Particles move but the mean settles
entries.lens: expectation versus fluctuating equilibrium counts

entries.sourceText: - **154. Mouse in a maze** \[Predict\]: guess the expected time to reach the cheese for a randomly wandering mouse.
entries.title: A maze reduced to a corridor
entries.lens: the absorbing-boundary corridor model

entries.sourceText: - **155. Birth and death** \[Slider\]: set birth and death rates and watch a small population boom or go extinct.
entries.title: Expected growth can hide extinction
entries.lens: the per-capita rates in a mean population model

entries.sourceText: - **156. Dying surnames** \[Predict\]: even growing populations lose most family names over generations (Galton–Watson).
entries.title: A lineage can vanish as the mean grows
entries.lens: the offspring generating-function fixed point

entries.sourceText: - **157. Pólya's urn** \[Predict\]: draw a ball, add another of the same color. Final shares are random but lock in early.
entries.title: Reinforcement preserves expected share
entries.lens: the mean of reinforced paths rather than a deterministic limit

entries.sourceText: - **158. Rich get richer** \[Slider\]: grow a network where new nodes prefer popular ones and hubs emerge.
entries.title: A popular node attracts the next link
entries.lens: degree-proportional attachment

entries.sourceText: - **159. Giant component** \[Slider\]: add random links; at an average of one link per node, a giant cluster suddenly appears.
entries.title: An asymptotic giant-component equation
entries.lens: the Poisson branching fixed point

entries.sourceText: - **160. Forest fire** \[Slider\]: set tree density; fires burn through once density passes about 59% on a grid.
entries.title: One path through a toy forest
entries.lens: a single independent tree corridor rather than a grid threshold

entries.sourceText: - **161. Darts for π** \[Predict\]: throw random darts at a square with a circle inside; the hit ratio estimates π.
entries.title: Darts estimate a circle's area
entries.lens: the hit fraction and Monte Carlo sampling error

entries.sourceText: - **162. Buffon's needle** \[Predict\]: drop needles on striped floorboards and π appears again.
entries.title: Needle crossings need a denominator
entries.lens: the crossing fraction before any nonlinear pi transformation

entries.sourceText: - **163. Area of a lake** \[Slider\]: draw any shape, scatter points, and estimate its area.
entries.title: Scatter points over a bounded lake
entries.lens: the bounding-area scale in an area estimate

entries.sourceText: - **164. Slow convergence** \[Slider\]: 100× more samples buys only 10× more precision.
entries.title: A hundredfold sample buys tenfold SE
entries.lens: the square-root Monte Carlo error scale

entries.sourceText: - **165. Will I make the train?** \[Slider\]: set variable walking, bus and transfer times; get your on-time probability.
entries.title: Enough successful transfer stages
entries.lens: the probability of a specified minimum number of successes

entries.sourceText: - **166. Project deadline** \[Predict\]: add up uncertain task durations; the realistic finish date sits well past the sum of the averages.
entries.title: Add uncertain task times correctly
entries.lens: expected duration versus a high-reliability deadline

entries.sourceText: - **167. Retirement plan** \[Slider\]: simulate thousands of market paths and see the chance your savings last.
entries.title: A single retirement return assumption
entries.lens: the stated constant-return path rather than a survival guarantee

entries.sourceText: - **168. Bracket simulator** \[Predict\]: simulate a tournament 10,000 times; even the favorite usually doesn't win.
entries.title: The favorite must survive each round
entries.lens: multiplication across independent tournament rounds

entries.sourceText: - **169. Rejection sampling** \[Slider\]: sample a strange shape by throwing points and keeping those under the curve.
entries.title: How many proposals survive rejection?
entries.lens: the accepted area under a uniform proposal

entries.sourceText: - **170. Inverse transform** \[Slider\]: turn uniform random numbers into any distribution through its CDF.
entries.title: Turn a uniform draw into a wait
entries.lens: the inverse exponential CDF

entries.sourceText: - **171. Rare-event sampling** \[Slider\]: importance sampling estimates a one-in-a-million event without a million tries.
entries.title: Oversample, then correct the weight
entries.lens: the proposal-to-target likelihood correction

entries.sourceText: - **172. Broken shuffle** \[Gotcha\]: a naive card-swap shuffle makes some orders more likely, and the histogram exposes it.
entries.title: A correct shuffle needs equal inclusion
entries.lens: the single-card position probability required by a uniform shuffle

entries.sourceText: - **173. Simulated annealing** \[Slider\]: cool slowly and a random search finds a short delivery route.
entries.title: Accept an uphill move while warm
entries.lens: the temperature in a stated annealing acceptance rule

entries.sourceText: - **174. Vanishing ball** \[Gotcha\]: in high dimensions, almost no random points in a cube land inside the inscribed ball.
entries.title: The inscribed ball loses cube volume
entries.lens: the uniform cube-to-ball volume ratio

entries.sourceText: - **175. Everyone is far away** \[Gotcha\]: in high dimensions, random points are all roughly the same distance apart.
entries.title: Distance scale in a larger cube
entries.lens: the root-mean-square distance between uniform points

entries.sourceText: - **176. Live win probability** \[Predict\]: simulate the rest of a match from the current score and watch the odds swing.
entries.title: A live game with shots remaining
entries.lens: the successes still needed in a finite horizon

entries.sourceText: - **177. π from fractions** \[Predict\]: the chance two random integers share no factor is 6/π² ≈ 61%.
entries.title: Count coprime pairs before the limit
entries.lens: the finite integer sampling range

entries.sourceText: - **178. Reservoir sampling** \[Slider\]: pick a fair random sample from a stream without knowing its length.
entries.title: A fair sample from a completed stream
entries.lens: the reservoir's uniform final inclusion probability

entries.sourceText: - **179. Random vs quasi-random** \[Split\]: scattered random points vs evenly spread Sobol points; the second estimates faster.
entries.title: Coverage under a random design
entries.lens: the empty-cell baseline before comparing a structured sampler

entries.sourceText: - **180. The house always wins** \[Slider\]: a small edge per bet becomes near-certain profit over millions of bets.
entries.title: A small edge over many bets
entries.lens: mean profit versus its finite-run spread

entries.sourceText: - **181. Language detector** \[Predict\]: type a sentence; a letter-pair Naive Bayes model guesses the language with probabilities.
entries.title: A toy language feature changes odds
entries.lens: the feature likelihood ratio in a two-language model

entries.sourceText: - **182. Logistic curve** \[Slider\]: drag weights and watch a straight score bend into a probability between 0 and 1.
entries.title: A straight score becomes a probability
entries.lens: the logistic link applied to an explicit score

entries.sourceText: - **183. Fit the boundary** \[Slider\]: move two Gaussian clouds and watch the best possible classifier boundary curve between them.
entries.title: Two Gaussian classes overlap
entries.lens: class densities and priors at one specified point

entries.sourceText: - **184. K-means vs mixtures** \[Split\]: hard clusters vs soft membership probabilities on the same overlapping data.
entries.title: A hard cluster hides soft membership
entries.lens: the posterior membership under equal-variance Gaussian classes

entries.sourceText: - **185. The dishonest casino** \[Predict\]: watch a dice sequence and guess when the loaded die was used; a hidden Markov model does better.
entries.title: A six can suggest a loaded die
entries.lens: the hidden-state prior before a specified die outcome

entries.sourceText: - **186. People like you** \[Slider\]: rate a few films and see predicted ratings with uncertainty from similar users.
entries.title: A neighbor rating with little evidence
entries.lens: the weight of sparse ratings in a stated blend

entries.sourceText: - **187. Next word** \[Predict\]: guess the next word in a sentence, then see a language model's probability ranking.
entries.title: Two candidate next words
entries.lens: the normalized probabilities of an explicit two-word model

entries.sourceText: - **188. Temperature** \[Slider\]: raise sampling temperature and watch text go from dull to creative to nonsense.
entries.title: Temperature flattens the same logits
entries.lens: the sampling concentration with fixed model scores

entries.sourceText: - **189. Top-p sampling** \[Slider\]: shrink the candidate pool and see repetition rise and weirdness fall.
entries.title: Keep the smallest probability prefix
entries.lens: the retained mass and renormalization in top-p sampling

entries.sourceText: - **190. Confident and wrong** \[Gotcha\]: an image classifier labels random noise as a specific animal with 99% confidence.
entries.title: High scores can be wrong often
entries.lens: the gap between a model score and observed correctness

entries.sourceText: - **191. Dropout uncertainty** \[Slider\]: run the same input through a network many times with dropout and see the spread.
entries.title: Three dropout predictions disagree
entries.lens: the spread of repeated model predictions

entries.sourceText: - **192. Ask the committee** \[Slider\]: train five models; where they disagree is where to distrust them.
entries.title: The committee can agree and err
entries.lens: prediction disagreement without an accuracy guarantee

entries.sourceText: - **193. Error bars widen** \[Slider\]: drag a prediction point away from the data and watch uncertainty balloon.
entries.title: Predict farther from the training mean
entries.lens: leverage in a specified linear prediction model

entries.sourceText: - **194. Spot the anomaly** \[Slider\]: fit a density to normal transactions; low-probability ones get flagged.
entries.title: Rare under a model is an anomaly score
entries.lens: the negative log probability under the fitted model

entries.sourceText: - **195. Hidden topics** \[Predict\]: guess the themes in a pile of headlines, then see what a topic model finds.
entries.title: Two toy headline themes
entries.lens: the topic prior behind an observed-word likelihood ratio

entries.sourceText: - **196. Keyboard autocomplete** \[Measure\]: type a phrase and see how many keystrokes prediction saved you.
entries.title: Count the keystrokes actually saved
entries.lens: the metric boundary for an autocomplete saving

entries.sourceText: - **197. Softmax isn't confidence** \[Gotcha\]: a 0.9 softmax score may be right far less than 90% of the time.
entries.title: Softmax scores need outcome checks
entries.lens: calibration rather than normalization alone

entries.sourceText: - **198. 99% accurate, useless** \[Gotcha\]: with 1% fraud, "never fraud" scores 99% accuracy and catches nothing.
entries.title: Always negative still scores highly
entries.lens: the rare-class base rate behind apparent accuracy

entries.sourceText: - **199. Precision vs recall** \[Slider\]: move the decision threshold and trade missed cases against false alarms.
entries.title: Precision and recall use different sets
entries.lens: the threshold's true-positive and false-positive tradeoff

entries.sourceText: - **200. Where should the line go?** \[Slider\]: change the cost of each mistake and watch the best threshold move.
entries.title: Change the cost of a missed case
entries.lens: the explicit costs assigned to two error types
